Longitudinal gait assessment in a stiff person syndrome
Tommaso Schirinzia,b,*, Andrea Sancesario a,b,*, Alberto Romano a,
Martina Favetta a, Marina Gobbi c, Massimiliano Valeriani a, Enrico S. Bertini a,
Enrico Castelli a, Gessica Vasco a, Maurizio Petrarca a and Gessica Della Bella a
Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is an autoimmune disorder with
multiple clinical presentations, all characterized by
generalized or focal muscular stiffness leading to abnormal
postures and movements. To date, no standardized
treatments are available; also, the outcome measures are
mainly clinical based and unstandardized, limiting the
reliability of clinical trials. In this case study, we used the
eight-camera motion capture system for gait analysis (GA) to
outline the gait features and track the clinical evolution of a
young patient with SPS receiving a personalized multimodal
therapy. GA was accurate in reflecting clinical changes over a
7-week-long period, thus representing a potential source for
objective biomarkers in SPS. Therefore, future studies
focusing on either the natural history or the treatment of SPS
could adopt GA for reliable outocome measures, confirming
this preliminary observation.

Introduction
Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is an autoimmune move-
ment disorder with a heterogeneous clinical spectrum,
including generalized, focal, or even fatal (progressive
encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus) pre-
sentations, all characterized by the increase in muscular
tone (stiffness). Antiglutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-
GAD) antibodies probably play a central role in causing
the disease, although the precise mechanisms are essentially
unknown (Balintet al., 2018).
Patients with SPS usually present stiffness in the prox-
imal muscles, superimposed painful spasms, hyper-
ekplexia (exaggerated startle response), and an increase
in serum anti-GAD antibodies (Balint et al. , 2018).
Unfortunately, data on natural history of the disease are
poor; also, the treatments are still unstandardized, based
on either etiological (steroids, intravenous immunoglo-
bulins) or symptomatic (muscle relaxants) approaches
(Bhatti and Gazali, 2015), both supported by physical
therapy (Potter, 2006; Hegyi, 2011). However, scientific
interest in this field is growing, and some randomized-

controlled trials have been finally conducted, with as yet
unsuccessful results. The advent of clinical trials on SPS
inevitably highlights the need for reliable and accurate
disease indexes, monitoring the clinical progression, as all
the current outcome measures are clinical-based scoring
systems and questionnaires (Dalakas et al. , 2017). In this
respect, here, we report on a young boy with SPS, whose
clinical evolution and response to an interesting com-
bined therapy were both tracked by gait analysis (GA).
Case description
The patient was a 12-year-old boy, healthy, with an
unremarkable medical and family history. He initially
presented with mild complaints and painful sensations
within the distal part of the right lower limb. Over
1 month, the symptomatology increased gradually in
intensity and spread along the entire limb and the trunk;
finally, generalized stiffness and confusion suddenly
appeared, leading to hospital admission. At the first
neurological examination, the mental status was altered,
with agitation, confusion, and abnormal perceptions.
Muscular tone was augmented, with severe generalized
stiffness (higher in the right lower limb) combined with
overt pyramidal signs (bilateral hyperreflexia and clonus,
Babinski sign on the right side). Hyperthermia and
rhabdomyolysis occurred, requiring specific treatments.
Diagnostic work-up included brain-spine MRI and
electroencephalography, which were normal; cerebro-
spinal fluid analysis, showing 32 leukocytes/ μl and
greater than six oligoclonal bands, with negative infective
tests; and spine radiographies showing Scheuermann
kyphosis (46 °) and S-shape left convex scoliosis (apex at
T1, 18 °), which were not present before. SPS was thus
suspected and the presence of anti-GAD antibodies was
measured in the cerebrospinal fluid (46.9 UI/ml) and
in the serum (1 : 200). Further investigations excluded

secondary causes, such as neoplasia or autoimmune dis-
orders. Intravenous immunoglobulin infusion (400 mg/
kg/day) and intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/day)
were started immediately at admission for 3 days, fol-
lowed by oral prednisone downtitration (2 weeks).
Several benzodiazepines (intravenous midazolam, oral
clonazepam, and lorazepam) and oral baclofen (started at
0.7 mg/kg/day and increased gradually ≥ 1.4 mg/kg/day)
were administered chronically as a muscle relaxant. The
clinical condition improved progressively; 5 weeks after
admission, the patient recovered autonomous standing
and walking, although with axial and limbs stiffness
(worse on the right side), peculiar head, trunk and limb
postures, and hyperekplexia. He was started on an
intensive program of neurorehabilitation and the first GA
was performed (T0). The rehabilitation program involved
a 90 min daily session, 6 days, for a week. The therapeutic
approach included low-intensity static stretching of the upper
and lower limbs, neck, and lumbar spinal muscle aimed at
reducing muscular contraction, improve articular range of
motion (ROM), and correct postural abnormalities. Exercises
aimed at improving balance and postural reactions with the
aid of oscillatory boards; walking training was performed with
a progressive improvement in distance and course difficulty,
until stair climbing training. Four weeks later, stiffness
reduced and locomotor abilities ameliorated, together with
pain and cramps, and the second GA was run (T1). With the
persistence of the neck stiffness with tiny right lateral incli-
nation together with adducted-internal rotated shoulder,
extended elbow, and extended knee on the right side, the
patient restarted steroid therapy with prednisone (50 mg/day)
and also received botulinum toxin A injections. Two hun-
dred UI BTX-A (Incobotulinumtoxin A, Xeomin) was used
and each vial of 100 units was reconstituted with 2 ml of

preservative-free 0.9% sodium chloride. BTX-A was injected
into the right Trapezius (30 UI), Teres Major (30 UI),
Pectoralis Major (30 UI), Triceps (60 UI), and Rectus
Femoris (50 UI). Medical and physical therapy continued
unchanged. After 3 weeks, slight stiffness and mild pyr-
amidal signs were present in the right limbs, but absent in
the left limbs and the third GA was acquired (T2). At this
time, the patient was able to move, run, and jump freely,
without any sensory complaints; he also regained self-
autonomy in daily activities and there was a significant
improvement in both mood and quality of life (global clinical
impression – severity was = 5; global clinical impression –
improvement was= 1); Therefore, the family was reassured
and satisfied by the good outcome. GA was conducted using
an eight-camera motion capture system (Vicon MX; Vicon
Motion Systems Ltd., UK) and two force plates (AMTI, Or6-
6; Berkshire, England) following the standard protocol
described previously (Vasco et al. , 2016). Kinematic para-
meters from consecutive GAs were thus analyzed qualita-
tively and quantitatively by repeated-measure analysis of
variance. At T1, the sagittal plane ROM of bilateral major
limb joints (shoulder, elbow, hip, and knee) improved sig-
nificantly, such as the stride/step time. At T2, previous
improvement was maintained and was further increased in
the elbow and knee (Fig. 1a and b). Moreover, radiological
assessment showed a slight improvement in both kyphosis
(42°) and scoliosis (15 °). All procedures followed Good
Clinical Practice guideline s. The study was carried out
according to the ethical principles of the Helsinki
Declaration. The patient provided consent for the case
description.
Discussion
In this case, comparative GA was used to follow up a
patient with SPS, receiving treatment with immunomo-
dulation, local, and systemic antispastic medications, and
physical exercise over a 7-week-long period. At the first
GA assessment (T0), the generalized stiffness led to
abnormal postures and limited walking activity with poor
ROM in several joints. Successive clinical improvement
because of a combined, personalized treatment then
resulted in parallel changes in GA parameters (Fig. 1a
and b), suggesting that GA may objectively track the
symptoms’ burden and the evolution of SPS, eventually
providing outcome measures. Definitely, more observa-
tions are mandatory to confirm the data.
Conclusion
SPS is a complex and challenging condition, and still
lacking standardized treatments and reliable outcome
measures. This case provide a preliminary observation on
the parallels between the overall clinical condition,
locomotor ability, and GA parameters in SPS to consider
GA as a possible source for objective disease biomarkers,
although limited by the time-consuming and cost of the
procedure. In addition, we also reported for the first time
the gait pattern in SPS and further confirmed the use-
fulness of a multimodal therapy, including physical
exercise, systemic, and local medications.
